To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the proposed approach outperforms state-of-the-art aggregation techniques, (2) it is robust to different types of document representations and (3) it is able to leverage document information even if the topic of the query is not explicitly mentioned in the text.

1) we can use document content as a proxy for worker reliability, 2) we can use this information for smoothing the distribution of labels across the similarity of the documents and, 3) we can use the resulting distribution to aggregate votes in a principled way.

(i) the clustering hypothesis can be exploited for efficient aggregation of crowdsourced votes, (ii) document similarity information can be used to propagate votes to similar documents in the corpus, (iii) this approach can improve the quality of the aggregation process and (iv) the approach can also be used as a means to estimate the similarity between documents.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether document information can be used for the aggregation of crowdsourcing votes.
the question of how to improve the efficiency of aggregation by exploiting information that is available from the documents themselves, without the need of additional behavioral features.
two main questions: How to exploit document content for the aggregation of crowd-generated relevance labels and how does the proposed aggregation scheme affect the quality of relevance labels?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed approach is a novel and effective method to aggregate relevance judgments from crowdsourced workers.
the proposed approach outperforms the baseline aggregation scheme, which uses a weighted majority voting, by 2% on the TREC 2012 Web track data set and by 1% on the TAC 2013 Microblog track data set.
we propose a novel approach that leverages document content to efficiently aggregate crowdsourcing votes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
document content can be exploited to enhance the quality of crowd-based relevance assessments.
we are exploiting the content of documents to aggregate the votes of crowd workers.
we are proposing to aggregate relevance judgments of crowdsourced workers based on the similarity between the documents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in addition to worker reliability features, we can exploit document content to improve the aggregation of crowd-generated relevance judgments.
document content can be leveraged for quality assurance in crowdsourcing tasks.
the use of document similarity can significantly improve the quality of aggregation, while at the same time reducing the need for worker reliability estimation.
